by: Draft for team review · written by a language model from engineers' public reports · checked in code
dek: Opus 5 earns the stronger case for planning and long chains, but Sonnet 5 can carry execution at lower token rates. Both can fail before model quality matters: adapter settings, note handoffs, and unfinished software.
rel: Gemini 3.8 Flash: fast coding, uneven judgment beyond the patch
MiniMax M3 review: strong coding, uneven reliability
GPT-6 Astra in Production: The Agent Is Better, the System Still Decides

body.text: One model plans; the other can carry the build

body: The sharpest reported difference: Opus 5 planned a project, while Sonnet 5 executed it. A dev.to engineer wrote «Opus 5 first drew up a plan, which the cheaper Claude Sonnet 5 (also on High effort) then executed.» That division gives you a useful starting point, not a model ranking.

We retraced the engineer’s test: Opus planned a system for training sessions, workers, orders, and certificates; Sonnet then executed the plan. The engineer wrote «Over the next few prompts, I gave Opus 5 more detail about the bugs, the architecture and the requirements.» Iterative feedback followed, and the project was finished in a person-day.
Opus 5 first drew up a plan, which the cheaper Claude Sonnet 5 (also on High effort) then executed.

The resulting application included connected business entities, working forms, and participant surveys. It also left broken invoice and project buttons, a faulty order refresh path, and certificate-generation trouble. The engineer’s report says «Some functionality was missing, though: certificate generation, statistics and the externally accessible survey were all in the specification but hadn't been implemented.»

We agree with the split, but only as a starting hypothesis. Planning and execution are different jobs, and the experiment used them that way. It does not isolate model effects: the engineer reported iterative feedback and different roles, not a matched trial. Your coding agent should measure accepted changes, not code volume.

body.caption: A split planning-and-execution workflow keeps model roles explicit and inserts a review gate.

body.text: Sonnet writes a weaker handoff; Opus writes a stronger note

body: For compact explanations passed between agents, Opus 5 wins this particular test; Sonnet 5 wins at learning the examples in the first place. A dev.to benchmark separated learning a rule from writing a short note that another model could use. That distinction matters in coding agents, where summaries become the next worker’s entire context. We retraced the test’s two stages: «Sonnet 5 learned the set at 0.92 and taught it at 0.75.»

body.alt: An engineer checks a handoff note against contradictory examples.
body.caption: A handoff must survive a fresh reader, not just its author.

body: The benchmark author reported Sonnet «learned the set at 0.92 and taught it at 0.75.» One note misstated a rule despite examples that contradicted it. Opus learned at 0.78, yet its notes scored 0.99. These are results from a synthetic hidden-rule task, not repository coding.
learned the set at 0.92 and taught it at 0.75.

Opus’s result is not a general victory. The same report describes empty replies when Opus read notes, including perfect notes. The author says «Empty replies on 9 of 12 perfect notes, and on 129 of 296 model notes.» A model that writes a helpful handoff but sometimes gives no answer still needs an explicit completion check.

We agree with the benchmark’s separation of authoring from reading. Do not grade a summarizer by its own answer alone. In your pipeline, ask a fresh worker to recover the requirements from the handoff, then test the resulting change. Preserve the original task and acceptance checks outside the generated summary.

body.text: Contrarian tone taxes both models, but Opus draws more fire

body: Neither model has a clear win on conversational friction; Sonnet 5 looks like the less severe choice in one comparison. A Hacker News commenter says «5 for sure is unbearable, 4.8 is a reasonable sweet spot» and ties continued Opus 5 use to better tool use. The same commenter writes «I just accept the cost of Fable for chatting and hope Opus 5.1 fixes this mess.»

A separate Reddit discussion, shown here as an embedded post, describes complaints about both Opus and Sonnet 5. That is opinion, not a controlled tone evaluation. Still, the split matters operationally. A coding assistant that disputes a premise or adds long qualifications can waste review time, even when its patch is sound.
5 for sure is unbearable, 4.8 is a reasonable sweet spot

We agree that style belongs in production evaluation, not only user research. We do not conclude that Sonnet is pleasant by default: the Reddit post includes it too. Instead, test your prompts against correction behavior, concise reporting, and willingness to follow a reaffirmed instruction. Keep the test tied to actual tasks.

Keep tone policies in the harness and score observable behavior. Ask the model to identify a real conflict, distinguish it from a preference, and continue when you confirm the request. If you need user-facing prose, have reviewers assess friction alongside factual and task accuracy.

body.text: A shared temperature setting can break both provider routes

body: Neither Opus 5 nor Sonnet 5 wins if the adapter forwards a rejected sampling setting. On Bedrock, a GitHub report describes 400 errors for Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 when shared settings include temperature or top-p. A separate LangChain issue reports the same class of rejection through its Anthropic adapter.

body.alt: A provider adapter rejects an unsupported setting before a model request.
body.caption: Adapter behavior can block a model request before generation begins.

body: The Bedrock engineer says «every request with a sampling setting hard-fails with a 400 on the Claude 5 generation over Bedrock». The report traces this to a profile flag that the adapter did not enforce. Another GitHub issue says «The package already knows which models these are» but request construction still forwarded the values.
every request with a sampling setting hard-fails with a 400 on the Claude 5 generation over Bedrock

This is where we disagree with model-only diagnosis. The failures do not show that either model reasons poorly; they show that a configuration contract and its adapter disagreed. The reports describe different integrations. Fixing one does not prove the other route is safe.

Treat model settings as provider-specific. Remove unsupported fields only when the selected model profile requires it, emit a visible warning, and add a regression test for each adapter. The Bedrock report offers an Anthropic route or removing the settings as workarounds. Do not assume a shared configuration works after a model switch.

body.caption: A model profile must govern settings before the provider adapter builds its request.

body.text: Opus 5 has a stronger planning case, not a self-validating patch

body: Opus 5 comes out ahead for broad planning; neither model earns autonomous write authority from these reports. The business-software experiment produced a substantial working application, but the remaining defects included actions that did nothing and a refresh path that broke an order. The interface looked finished before every workflow did.

body.alt: An engineer tests a polished application and finds a broken workflow.
body.caption: A convincing interface does not certify every workflow.

body: The engineer’s conclusion was «yes, building business software is much easier now, and the result can be reliable.» The caveat is right there: certificate generation failed, possibly due to a package issue, and some generated buttons did not work. The experiment explicitly excluded code quality and readability.
yes, building business software is much easier now, and the result can be reliable.

Sonnet’s execution role in that project does not prove it is safer or less capable. The engineer fed Opus further bug and requirement details across prompts. That human feedback loop helped close gaps; it is part of the result, not noise to remove from the story.

We agree with the practical conclusion and reject the stronger version that a successful demo means production readiness. Keep generated writes behind review. Exercise refreshes, external access, persistence, and integrations in the actual environment. A polished interface can conceal a broken workflow.

body.text: Sonnet costs less per token; retries can erase the advantage

body: Sonnet 5 wins on listed token rates; Opus 5 needs to justify its premium with accepted work. The registry rate card shows lower input and output rates for Sonnet. Cached input is lower too. The gap changes the default, not the architecture.

That makes Sonnet the natural candidate for repeated, bounded execution, not a guaranteed cheaper outcome. Failed notes, retries, long explanations, and review all consume budget. Opus can be cheaper per accepted result if it prevents enough downstream repair, but the available experiments do not establish that for your workload.

A dev.to agent guide recommends Sonnet for ordinary multi-source work and Opus for long chains. We agree with the task distinction, not any blanket model tier. Its recommendation is practitioner guidance, not matched accounting of retries, latency, or reviewer time.

Track input, output, cached tokens, retries, tool calls, and accepted changes by task class. For Claude Opus 5 vs Claude Sonnet 5 pricing, compare cost per accepted outcome. Do not reduce the decision to per-million-token rates.

body.text: Opus and Sonnet share a million-token ceiling, not demonstrated recall

body: Neither model wins on advertised context capacity: both are listed with a one-million-token window. That equality settles only the published ceiling. None of the head-to-head engineering evidence here compares their recall, retrieval quality, or performance across a long production session.

The note benchmark did test information transfer, but it used short notes and fresh readers, not million-token contexts. Its important finding is narrower: a correct internal state can become a wrong written handoff. More context would not automatically repair that boundary.

The Reddit discussion about system prompts reports captures for both models, but it is not a context-window test. It describes different prompt templates and behavior instructions, not measured recall under matched long inputs. We use it as a reason to inspect runtime assembly, not rank context quality.

Measure the context you actually retain after tool schemas, conversation history, and generated summaries. Run retrieval probes at realistic positions and inspect the answer’s evidence. Keep durable state outside the model’s transient context when a missed detail could break a task.

body.text: Provider availability remains unresolved under matched load

body: Sonnet 5 wins in one observed Zen outage window; the evidence is too narrow to call it more reliable overall. A GitHub report says Opus intermittently returned 503 responses through Zen while Sonnet succeeded with the same key, endpoint, network, and request shape.

The reporter’s reproduction changed only the model in the request: «Repeat with only the model changed to `claude-sonnet-5`; Sonnet returns HTTP 200.» The same report says Opus sometimes returned 200 amid repeated 503 responses. This isolates a route-specific episode, not a general availability comparison.

We agree that fallback must be designed at the provider boundary. We are not convinced that this establishes a model reliability ranking: the post points to an upstream route, and no matched duration or failure rate is available. A model name alone cannot tell you which endpoint is healthy now.

To settle this, measure successful completions, error classes, retry recovery, and latency for both models through your actual provider path. Preserve request shape and workload. Until then, use bounded retries and a fallback route, and expose provider errors distinctly from model-quality failures.

body: Which is better for coding, Claude Opus 5 or Claude Sonnet 5?

Claude Opus 5 has the stronger reported case for planning complex work, while Claude Sonnet 5 has a practical case for executing bounded tasks. In the dev.to experiment, Opus planned and Sonnet implemented business software, but defects remained. Treat this as a workflow example, not a controlled coding benchmark; compare accepted patches, repair effort, and test results on your own repository.
Is Claude Sonnet 5 cheaper than Claude Opus 5?

Yes, Sonnet 5 has lower listed input, output, and cached-input token rates than Opus 5. Those rates do not include retries, tool usage, review, or the cost of defects. Track total spend and human time per accepted task before deciding that the lower token rate produces a lower production cost.
Why does Claude Opus 5 return a 400 error with temperature?

A provider adapter may forward sampling settings that the selected model rejects. GitHub reports describe temperature and related settings causing 400 responses through Anthropic and Bedrock integrations, despite model profiles carrying relevant support information. Check the exact provider path, remove unsupported settings or filter them by profile, and add a regression test before switching traffic.
